title: WebOps Commander
pitch: An agent-native incident response command center where AI agents investigate outages through WebMCP, simulate safe fixes, and execute production-changing actions only after explicit human approval.

 Inspiration 

 Modern websites are designed primarily for people. When AI agents need to interact with those applications, they often have to interpret pages visually, reason about buttons and forms, and reproduce workflows that were never designed for machine interaction. 

 WebMCP suggests a different future: websites can expose intentional, structured capabilities directly to AI agents while continuing to provide rich interfaces for humans. 

 That idea inspired WebOps Commander . 

 We wanted to explore a question: 

 
 What would an incident-response application look like if it were designed for humans and AI agents from the beginning? 
 

 Instead of building another chatbot or allowing an agent to blindly click through an operations dashboard, WebOps Commander gives the agent structured operational capabilities through WebMCP while preserving explicit human control over consequential actions. 

 What it does 

 WebOps Commander is an agent-native incident-response command center built around a deterministic simulated production outage. 

 A fictional e-commerce platform experiences a severe checkout incident shortly after a new version of checkout-service is deployed. 

 The human operator sees a visual operations dashboard containing: 

 
 live service health 
 checkout error rate 
 p95 latency 
 order throughput 
 estimated revenue impact 
 service dependencies 
 logs 
 distributed traces 
 deployment history 
 incident status 
 agent activity 
 

 At the same time, a compatible AI agent receives structured WebMCP tools that allow it to investigate the same system directly. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the active incident 
 inspect service health 
 query metrics 
 search logs 
 inspect traces 
 inspect service dependencies 
 inspect recent deployments 
 compare releases 
 search operational runbooks 
 estimate customer impact 
 simulate a rollback 
 request a production-changing action 
 wait for explicit human approval 
 execute an approved rollback 
 observe system recovery 
 update and resolve the incident 
 

 The core workflow is: 

 Observe → Investigate → Correlate → Simulate → Request Approval → Human Approves → Execute → Recover 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent interacting with an operations platform may need to determine which page contains deployment information, interpret charts, find buttons, understand forms, and infer what actions are safe to perform. 

 That approach can be brittle. 

 With WebMCP, WebOps Commander intentionally exposes structured capabilities such as: 

 query_service_metrics 

 search_logs 

 search_traces 

 get_recent_deployments 

 compare_deployments 

 simulate_rollback 

 request_rollback 

 execute_approved_action 

 The agent does not need to guess how the user interface works. 

 The website tells the agent what capabilities are available, what inputs they accept, and what actions are permitted. 

 The human interface and agent interface operate on the same application state, so WebMCP actions are immediately visible inside the command center. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally not designed around full autonomy. 

 Investigation is safe for the agent to perform independently. 

 Consequential actions are different. 

 For example, the agent can determine that a rollback is likely to resolve the incident and simulate its expected impact, but it cannot immediately change the simulated production environment. 

 Instead, it creates a pending action: 

 Rollback checkout-service from v2.18.4 to v2.18.3 

 The human sees the proposed action together with: 

 
 the agent's reasoning 
 expected recovery 
 current error rate 
 expected post-rollback error rate 
 estimated risk 
 

 The human can then approve or reject the action. 

 Only an approved action can be executed. 

 This creates a clear separation between: 

 Agent investigation 

 Agent recommendation 

 Human authorization 

 Agent execution 

 Every WebMCP interaction is also recorded in the visible agent activity timeline. 

 The Incident 

 The demonstration focuses on one deliberately small but polished scenario: Checkout Meltdown . 

 A deployment of checkout-service v2.18.4 introduces stricter payment-token issuer validation. 

 Shortly afterward: 

 
 checkout failures increase from approximately 0.6% to 18.4% 
 p95 checkout latency increases from approximately 620 ms to 4.7 seconds 
 completed orders fall by approximately 38% 
 estimated revenue exposure reaches approximately $21.4K per simulated minute 
 

 Other services remain healthy. 

 Through metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and release comparison, the agent can correlate the incident with v2.18.4 . 

 It can then simulate a rollback to v2.18.3 , request authorization, and—after human approval—execute the remediation. 

 The command center visually shows the system recovering. 

 How we are building it 

 WebOps Commander is intentionally scoped as a focused hackathon demonstration rather than a production observability platform. 

 The application uses a deterministic simulation instead of real cloud infrastructure so that every judge can reproduce the same incident without accounts, API keys, external services, or unreliable dependencies. 

 The planned architecture consists of: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 shadcn/ui 
 WebMCP 
 Zod 
 Zustand 
 Recharts 
 Vitest 
 Playwright 
 GitHub Actions 
 

 Operational state, telemetry, logs, traces, deployments, and recovery behavior are simulated locally. 

 WebMCP is the primary agent interface. 

 The project does not require an embedded chatbot or external LLM API—the compatible AI agent interacting with the website is the agent. 

 Challenges 

 The most interesting challenge is not simply exposing functions to an AI agent. 

 It is deciding what an agent should be allowed to do. 

 Read-only investigation tools should be easy to invoke. 

 Simulation should be safe. 

 Production-changing operations should be protected. 

 That led us to design a small capability model with separate categories for: 

 
 read operations 
 simulations 
 approval requests 
 consequential actions
